payload.throughline: Classify signal entry and hormone structure, then map endocrine source to cellular action.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: identify the membrane protein class from the first event after a signal arrives. This is low stakes; it does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: use the trigger and the first controlled step to distinguish four membrane-signaling mechanisms, then predict the immediate consequence before following any longer cascade.
Bridge from prior nervous-system organization: a signal must be sensed before an effector response can occur. Here, the membrane protein is the signal-entry element.

A voltage-gated ion channel responds to membrane potential. A ligand-gated ion channel responds when a chemical messenger binds. In both cases, gate opening changes membrane permeability and permits selected ions to move down their electrochemical gradients.
A receptor enzyme converts ligand binding into enzyme activity on the cytosolic side, often by phosphorylation. Its direct action is chemical modification, not formation of an ion-conducting pore.

A G protein–coupled receptor changes conformation and promotes GDP-for-GTP exchange on a heterotrimeric G protein. The activated G-protein subunits then regulate an effector. The receptor does not itself transport the ligand or act as an ion pore.

Mental model — Trigger → first controlled step → immediate consequence. Voltage or ligand can open a channel; ligand can activate an enzyme domain; ligand can activate a G protein through a G protein–coupled receptor.

Expert selection: if a prompt reports an ion current immediately after a gate opens, I choose a channel mechanism. If it reports receptor-side phosphorylation, I choose a receptor enzyme. If GDP/GTP exchange appears before an effector, I choose a G protein–coupled receptor. I rule out alternatives by locating the earliest stated event.

Worked example: an extracellular messenger binds a seven-pass membrane protein. The receptor changes shape, a G alpha subunit releases GDP and binds GTP, and an effector enzyme changes activity. The decisive cue is nucleotide exchange on a G protein, so the receptor is a G protein–coupled receptor. A ligand-gated channel is ruled out because no ion-conducting pore is the first controlled step; a receptor enzyme is ruled out because the receptor itself is not described as catalyzing phosphorylation.
Guided practice: name the trigger first, then identify the directly controlled membrane event.
Less help: use only the earliest intracellular consequence to classify the receptor.
On your own: distinguish a G protein–coupled receptor from a channel and a receptor enzyme without an answer-bearing hint.

Boundary: ligand binding does not automatically mean ligand-gated channel. Ask whether binding opens a pore, activates an enzyme function, or activates a G protein. A downstream ion change does not make every upstream receptor an ion channel.
Near exit: predict the direct effect of disrupting the gate-sensing machinery of a voltage-gated channel.
Changed-task exit: move from an ion-channel decision to a receptor–G-protein sequence and identify the earliest blocked step.

Targeted repair for the direct-mechanism function: locate the trigger, then ask what the membrane protein itself does. A channel changes permeability by opening a pore; an enzyme receptor catalyzes a chemical change; a G protein–coupled receptor activates a G protein.
Fresh exact re-entry: classify the immediate channel consequence in a new ligand, ion, and pore setting. No exposed item or answer is reused.

Targeted repair for the G-protein sequence: ligand binds receptor → receptor changes conformation → G alpha exchanges GDP for GTP → G-protein subunit regulates an effector. Stop at the first broken arrow.
Fresh exact re-entry: predict the first missing GPCR consequence in a new effector setting without reusing the exposed task.

Repair is bounded to one targeted cue and one fresh re-entry for each failed function. If the fresh check is still unresolved, the lesson returns control for later support and does not award exit success.

Recap and exit: retrieve the three-part test — trigger, first controlled step, immediate consequence. Use it to separate gated channels, receptor enzymes, and G protein–coupled receptors without tracing an unnecessary full cascade.
Starting check: use a compact structural description to predict how an endocrine signal can reach its receptor. This is low stakes and cannot satisfy an exit.
Goal: connect molecular structure to signaling behavior. Focus on steroid, terpene, and terpenoid structures only, then predict whether a membrane or intracellular receptor is plausible.

Steroids share a characteristic core of four fused carbon rings. Many steroid hormones have enough nonpolar surface to cross a phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors in the cytosol or nucleus; the hormone–receptor complex can regulate transcription.

Terpenes are assembled from five-carbon isoprene units. Terpenoids are modified terpene derivatives, commonly containing oxygen-bearing functional groups. Members of these families can participate in signaling or endocrine biology.

Structure constrains but does not uniquely determine receptor location. A largely nonpolar signal is more able to cross a membrane than a permanently charged signal, but experimental information about the receptor remains decisive.
Mental model — Structural scaffold → polarity and membrane passage → receptor location → cellular action. Keep each arrow conditional on the facts supplied in the task.

Expert selection: I first look for a four-fused-ring steroid core or a repeating isoprene-derived skeleton. Then I inspect polar or charged groups. I predict intracellular signaling only when membrane passage and an intracellular receptor are both supported; I do not treat every lipid-like molecule as a steroid.

Worked example: a hormone has four fused rings, few polar groups, and a receptor in the cytosol. Its steroid scaffold and low polarity support membrane passage. After binding, the receptor complex enters the nucleus and changes transcription. I rule out a membrane-channel mechanism because no pore or ion flux is described, and I do not call the molecule a terpene merely because both families are rich in carbon.
Guided practice: identify the scaffold, estimate membrane passage from polarity, then place the receptor.
Less help: distinguish an isoprene-derived scaffold from a steroid fused-ring core.
On your own: classify a modified terpene structure and connect it to a signaling role.

Boundary: lipid-soluble does not mean “must be a steroid,” and oxygen-containing does not mean “cannot cross a membrane.” Use the actual scaffold, charge, and receptor evidence. Broad fatty-acid and membrane-lipid chemistry is outside this KC.
Near exit: use a steroid scaffold and a disrupted intracellular receptor step to predict the most direct signaling consequence.
Changed-task exit: use an isoprene-derived, oxygenated signaling structure and a nuclear response to classify the structure–function relation.

Targeted repair for steroid-receptor consequence reasoning: confirm that the signal has entered the cell, identify the disrupted intracellular-receptor step, and then predict the first downstream output that step can no longer support. Do not return to membrane-passage reasoning once entry is stated.
Fresh exact re-entry: use a new intracellular-receptor disruption to predict the most direct steroid-signaling consequence.

Targeted repair for family distinction: steroid means a four-fused-ring core; terpene means an isoprene-unit carbon framework; terpenoid means a modified terpene derivative. Signaling role is a separate decision.
Fresh exact re-entry: classify a new oxygenated isoprene-derived messenger and connect it to an intracellular receptor observation.
Each failed function receives one targeted repair and one fresh item. A second miss returns control for later support; repair completion alone never counts as exit success.

Recap and exit: retrieve the chain scaffold → polarity → membrane passage → receptor location → action. Keep steroid and terpene/terpenoid classification separate from the final signaling-role prediction.

Prerequisite check from V3-LES-474771: order a sensor, central integration step, and effector output in a control loop. This low-stakes check activates the nervous-control bridge and cannot satisfy an endocrine exit.
If that sensor → integration → effector organization is unfamiliar, return to the prerequisite lesson before relying on the neuroendocrine examples.

Goal: build a location → gland → product → hormone-type map, then keep hormone synthesis distinct from storage and release. The nervous-system control-loop prerequisite supports the hypothalamus–pituitary bridge.

Endocrine glands release hormones into internal fluids rather than through ducts. A hormone affects only cells with the appropriate receptor. Peptide or protein hormones generally use membrane receptors; many steroids use intracellular receptors; amino-acid derivatives vary, so receptor location must be learned from the supplied hormone context.

Major source map: hypothalamus in the brain controls the pituitary and synthesizes vasopressin (ADH) and oxytocin; the posterior pituitary stores and releases those two hormones. The anterior pituitary produces hormones including TSH and ACTH. The thyroid in the anterior neck produces thyroid hormones; the parathyroids on its posterior surface produce parathyroid hormone.

The adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone; the adrenal medulla produces catecholamines such as epinephrine. Pancreatic islet beta cells produce insulin and alpha cells produce glucagon. Ovaries and testes produce major gonadal steroids; the pineal gland produces melatonin.

Mental model — Location → source tissue → synthesized product → release site → chemical class → receptor-bearing target. A single arrow may split, as in hypothalamic synthesis followed by posterior-pituitary release.

Expert selection: I refuse to map a hormone by name alone. I locate the tissue, separate synthesis from release, classify the hormone, and then use receptor information. For TSH, “thyroid” in the name is the target cue, not the source: the anterior pituitary is the source.

Worked example: compare three rows. Cortisol maps to adrenal cortex → steroid → intracellular-receptor signaling. Insulin maps to pancreatic beta cell → peptide → membrane-receptor signaling. ADH maps to hypothalamic synthesis → posterior-pituitary storage and release → peptide. The ADH row demonstrates why “where it is released” and “where it is made” cannot be collapsed.
Guided practice: use location, source, and target words to avoid assigning a tropic hormone to the gland it stimulates.
Less help: separate hypothalamic synthesis from posterior-pituitary release.
On your own: pair a major gland region with a hormone product and chemical type.

Boundary: a hormone name can identify its target without identifying its source. TSH targets the thyroid but is produced by the anterior pituitary. ADH and oxytocin are released from the posterior pituitary but synthesized in the hypothalamus. Do not create a separate KC for every gland or hormone.
Near exit: identify a major gland from location and product.
Changed-task exit: use a lesion in the hypothalamic–posterior-pituitary connection to distinguish synthesis from release.
Targeted repair for gland mapping: locate the organ first, separate cortex from medulla or anterior from posterior, then bind the specific product to that source.
Fresh exact re-entry: map a pancreatic cell source to its product in a new metabolic condition.
Targeted repair for neuroendocrine source logic: hypothalamic neurons synthesize ADH and oxytocin; axons carry them to the posterior pituitary; the posterior pituitary stores and releases them.
Fresh exact re-entry: infer the release consequence of reduced hypothalamic synthesis without reusing the lesion item.

If END-ACT-ENTRY does not show readiness for the sensor → integration → effector control-loop prerequisite, stop endocrine progression and return to the planner for canonical hard prerequisite V3-LES-474771 through relation V3-EDG-103186. This lesson does not author a prerequisite-support route.
If a bounded endocrine exit re-entry remains unresolved, also return to the planner without exit credit.
Recap and exit: retrieve one source map from each region — brain, neck, adrenal, pancreas, and gonad — and preserve the special hypothalamus-synthesis/posterior-pituitary-release distinction.
Lesson exit: continue to the required coordination capstones, where these component skills are applied together. The capstone content and evidence remain separate from this lesson candidate.
